01.note: A newly married man comes to Rabban Gamliel, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and says that on the wedding night he found no blood, implying his bride was not a virgin. The bride insists she was. Rabban Gamliel asks for the cloth they used, has it soaked and washed, and finds a few drops of blood on it. He tells the groom to go and enjoy his marriage, since she was a virgin after all.
01.why: The Gemara has been discussing how far a husband is believed when he claims his bride was not a virgin, with earlier cases brought to Rabban Gamliel. This case shows a judge testing the claim physically rather than accepting it; the Gemara then asks if such tests work in Babylonia.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, compiler of the Mishna; a leading Sage and judge in the Land of Israel.

terms.term: Go take possession of your acquisition
terms.meaning: A legal way of saying the marriage stands and the husband has no complaint: the wife he married is exactly what she was presented as.

02.note: The Sages recalled that Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai would dance before a bride holding a myrtle branch, praising her beauty. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak went further, juggling three myrtle branches as he danced, and Rabbi Zeira complained that the old man was embarrassing the scholars. But when Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak died, a pillar of fire separated him from everyone else, a sign tradition says is granted to only one or two people in a generation.
02.why: The Gemara is collecting examples of how Sages sang and danced to honor brides and scholars. This story shows a Sage's undignified wedding dancing being vindicated, and Rabbi Zeira's comment right after reads the pillar of fire as his reward for it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai
people.about: A leading Sage of the Mishna era, often praised in the Talmud for his piety.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel, remembered here as an old man who danced enthusiastically at weddings.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Babylonian-born Sage who moved to the Land of Israel; here he first criticizes the dancing.

terms.meaning: A fragrant evergreen branch, traditionally used at weddings and in celebrations.
A miraculous sign recalling the pillar of fire that guided Israel in the wilderness; here it marks the dead man as uniquely holy.

03.note: To settle a legal problem about witnesses who contradict each other, Rav Nahman points to an earlier case. A man called bar Shatya, who suffered bouts of insanity, sold his property. One pair of witnesses testified that he sold it while insane, and another pair that he sold it while sane. Rav Ashi ruled that the two testimonies cancel out and the property stays with bar Shatya, but only if he had inherited it from his fathers; if he had bought it himself, the sale stands.
03.why: The Gemara is debating whether witnesses can be contradicted when they are not present. Rav Nahman answers that two witnesses against two cancel out and the money stays with its owner, and the bar Shatya case is cited as the precedent for that rule.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage and judge, known for his rulings on civil law.

people.name: bar Shatya
people.about: A man with periodic bouts of insanity whose property sale became a legal test case; the name roughly means son of the madman.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A late Babylonian Sage, head of the academy at Sura, traditionally credited with editing the Talmud.

terms.meaning: When two pairs of equally valid witnesses contradict each other, the court treats both testimonies as cancelling out and acts as if neither had testified.
Property a person inherited, which gives him a strong presumption of ownership, unlike property he bought himself.

04.note: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Hiyya, was married to the daughter of Rabbi Yannai and studied away from home, returning every Friday at dusk; his father-in-law would see a pillar of fire going before him. One Friday he became absorbed in his studies and did not come home. Seeing no sign, Rabbi Yannai said to turn over his bed, as mourners do, since if Yehuda were alive he would never have missed his time with his wife. His words came true like an error spoken by a ruler, and Yehuda died.
04.why: The Gemara is discussing how often scholars must be home with their wives, and has said Friday night is their proper time. Like the story of Rav Rehumi just before it, this case warns of the danger of a scholar neglecting his wife for study.

people.name: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Son of the great Sage Rabbi Hiyya and son-in-law of Rabbi Yannai; a scholar who studied away from home.

people.name: Rabbi Yannai
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel and Yehuda's father-in-law, whose spoken words prove fatal.

terms.meaning: An ancient mourning custom: the beds in a house were overturned when a family member died.
The regular schedule a husband owes his wife for marital relations, which Jewish law treats as her right; for scholars it was Friday night.

05.note: Rav Yehuda, and an older teaching that agrees with him, tell how the marriage contract came to work as it does. At first a bride was promised 200 dinars, or 100 for a widow, but men grew old without marrying. The Sages had the money kept in the bride's father's house, but an angry husband could too easily say: go to your marriage contract. Then it was kept in the husband's house, where rich women made it into silver and gold baskets and poor women into a chamber pot, and husbands still said: take it and leave. Finally Shimon ben Shatah ruled that a husband writes that all his property guarantees the payment.
05.why: The Gemara has been discussing the mishna's rule about the husband's property and the marriage contract, and here gives the history of why all of a husband's property is pledged to pay it.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage, student of Rav and Shmuel.

people.name: Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: A leader of the Sages in the first century BCE, credited with many early rulings, including this one.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, a document listing what a husband owes his wife, above all a sum to be paid to her if he divorces her or dies.
A teaching from the era of the Mishna that was not included in the Mishna itself; the Gemara quotes these as support.
Silver coins; 200 dinars was a large sum, the standard minimum promised to a first-time bride.

06.note: Members of the household of the prince, the head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel, seized a maidservant belonging to orphans in an alley, as payment for a debt the orphans' father owed them. Rabbi Abbahu, sitting as a judge with two colleagues, told them the seizure was fine. Rabbi Abba, sitting with the judges, objected: were they flattering the prince's household? He reminded them that judges had once ruled this way, following Rabbi Tarfon, and Reish Lakish had reversed their ruling. The text does not say how the case ended.
06.why: The Gemara is collecting cases of creditors seizing property from orphans to pay their dead father's debts, and whether Rabbi Tarfon's view allowing this is followed. This case adds a reminder that Reish Lakish had overturned such a ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A leading Sage of Caesarea in the Land of Israel, known for his ties to the Roman authorities.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel, sitting as one of the three judges.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel; his name means the smith.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: A Babylonian-born Sage who settled in the Land of Israel; here he challenges the judges.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, a great Sage of the Land of Israel and Rabbi Yohanan's study partner and rival.

terms.meaning: The household of the Nasi, the official head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel; ruling against them took courage.
A Sage of the Mishna whose opinion lets a creditor keep property of a dead debtor that he has already seized, even from the orphans.

07.note: A man prayed behind the synagogue without turning to face it. Elijah the Prophet passed by and saw him, appearing to him as an Arab. He said to him: is this how you stand before your Master? Then he drew a sword and killed him.
07.why: Rav Huna has just said that one who prays behind the synagogue is called wicked, and Abaye limited this to someone who does not face the synagogue. The story shows how serious that offense is.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The biblical prophet, who in Talmudic stories returns to visit people, often in disguise.

terms.meaning: Praying outside the building facing away from it, so that he seems to turn his back on the congregation praying inside.
